difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: MODERATE because it applies one concept (what a single pass of each elementary sort does) through three short two-pass execution traces, a routine computation that takes a prepared student about two minutes.
stem:
Consider the following sorting algorithms:

(i) Bubble sort

(ii) Insertion sort

(iii) Selection sort

Which **ONE** among the following choices of sorting algorithms sorts the numbers in the array $[4, 3, 2, 1, 5]$ in increasing order after **exactly two** passes over the array?

solution.quick: Trace two passes of each algorithm on $[4, 3, 2, 1, 5]$. Bubble sort gives $[3, 2, 1, 4, 5] \to [2, 1, 3, 4, 5]$ and insertion sort gives $[3, 4, 2, 1, 5] \to [2, 3, 4, 1, 5]$; neither is sorted. Selection sort swaps the minimum to the front each pass: $[1, 3, 2, 4, 5] \to [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]$, sorted after exactly two passes. Only (iii) works, so the answer is **(B)**.

steps.title: What one pass of each algorithm does
steps.body:
The target is $[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]$. Use the standard textbook definition of a pass for each algorithm:

| Algorithm | One pass | Guarantee after $k$ passes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bubble sort | One left-to-right sweep that compares adjacent elements and swaps them if they are out of order | The $k$ largest elements sit in their final places at the right end |
| Insertion sort | Take the next element of the unsorted part and insert it into the sorted prefix | The first $k + 1$ elements are sorted among themselves; the rest are untouched |
| Selection sort | Find the minimum of the unsorted part and swap it into the first unsorted position | The $k$ smallest elements sit in their final places at the left end |

Now trace exactly two passes of each on $[4, 3, 2, 1, 5]$.

steps.title: (i) Bubble sort: two passes are not enough
steps.body:
**Pass 1** (compare positions $1\text{–}2, 2\text{–}3, 3\text{–}4, 4\text{–}5$):

| Compare | Swap? | Array |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $4, 3$ | Yes | $[3, 4, 2, 1, 5]$ |
| $4, 2$ | Yes | $[3, 2, 4, 1, 5]$ |
| $4, 1$ | Yes | $[3, 2, 1, 4, 5]$ |
| $4, 5$ | No | $[3, 2, 1, 4, 5]$ |

**Pass 2** ($5$ is already fixed, so compare positions $1\text{–}2, 2\text{–}3, 3\text{–}4$):

| Compare | Swap? | Array |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $3, 2$ | Yes | $[2, 3, 1, 4, 5]$ |
| $3, 1$ | Yes | $[2, 1, 3, 4, 5]$ |
| $3, 4$ | No | $[2, 1, 3, 4, 5]$ |

After two passes the array is $[2, 1, 3, 4, 5]$, which is **not sorted** ($2 > 1$). A third pass is needed. The reason: the element $1$ starts at position 4, and a left-to-right sweep moves a small element only **one** place left per pass, so $1$ needs $3$ passes to reach position 1. (Sweeping right-to-left instead gives $[1, 4, 3, 2, 5]$ and then $[1, 2, 4, 3, 5]$, also unsorted after two passes.)

steps.title: (ii) Insertion sort: two passes are not enough
steps.body:
The sorted prefix starts as $[4]$.

- **Pass 1:** insert $3$ into $[4]$. Since $3 < 4$, shift $4$ right: $[3, 4 \mid 2, 1, 5]$.
- **Pass 2:** insert $2$ into $[3, 4]$. Since $2 < 4$ and $2 < 3$, shift both right: $[2, 3, 4 \mid 1, 5]$.

After two passes the array is $[2, 3, 4, 1, 5]$, which is **not sorted**: the $1$ at position 4 has not even been looked at yet. It is inserted only in pass 3, giving $[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]$ (pass 4 then inserts $5$ without moving anything).

steps.title: (iii) Selection sort: sorted after exactly two passes
steps.body:
- **Pass 1:** the unsorted part is $[4, 3, 2, 1, 5]$. Its minimum is $1$ (position 4). Swap it with position 1: $[1 \mid 3, 2, 4, 5]$.
- **Pass 2:** the unsorted part is $[3, 2, 4, 5]$. Its minimum is $2$ (position 3). Swap it with position 2: $[1, 2 \mid 3, 4, 5]$.

After two passes the array is $[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]$, which **is sorted**. After one pass it was $[1, 3, 2, 4, 5]$, which is not, so the array becomes sorted after **exactly two** passes. The remaining passes find the minimum already in place and change nothing.

Why it works here: $[4, 3, 2, 1, 5]$ is the sorted array with two pairs exchanged ($1 \leftrightarrow 4$ and $2 \leftrightarrow 3$), and each selection-sort swap undoes one of those exchanges. (This is the standard version that selects the minimum. A variant that selects the maximum and swaps it to the end would give $[4, 3, 2, 1, 5]$ and then $[1, 3, 2, 4, 5]$, unsorted after two passes, and then no option would be correct.)

steps.title: Complexity note and conclusion
steps.body:
Each pass of all three algorithms scans the unsorted part, so a pass costs $O(n)$ comparisons and all three are $O(n^2)$ in the worst case. How many passes a particular input needs is what differs:

| Algorithm | After pass 1 | After pass 2 | Sorted after exactly two passes? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| (i) Bubble sort | $[3, 2, 1, 4, 5]$ | $[2, 1, 3, 4, 5]$ | No (needs 3) |
| (ii) Insertion sort | $[3, 4, 2, 1, 5]$ | $[2, 3, 4, 1, 5]$ | No (needs 3) |
| (iii) Selection sort | $[1, 3, 2, 4, 5]$ | $[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]$ | **Yes** |

Only (iii) works, so the answer is **(B)** "(iii) only".

solution.teaching:
**Three elementary sorts, and what a "pass" guarantees.** All three algorithms build a sorted region one pass at a time, but they build it differently, and that decides how many passes a given input needs.

- **Bubble sort** repeatedly sweeps left to right, swapping adjacent out-of-order pairs. Each sweep carries the largest remaining element to the end, like a bubble rising. So after $k$ passes the $k$ largest elements are final. Large elements move right quickly (many places per pass), but small elements move left only **one place per pass**. A small element far to the right (a "turtle") therefore forces many passes.
- **Insertion sort** grows a sorted prefix. Pass $k$ takes the element at position $k + 1$ and slides it left into its correct place within the prefix. After $k$ passes the first $k + 1$ elements are sorted among themselves, but nothing to their right has been examined yet, so a small element near the end is not placed until its own pass arrives.
- **Selection sort** grows a sorted prefix of *final* values. Each pass finds the minimum of the unsorted part and swaps it to the front of that part, with at most one swap per pass. After $k$ passes the $k$ smallest elements are in their final positions. If the rest happens to be in order already, the array is sorted early.

Two useful consequences. First, one selection-sort swap can put *two* elements into their final places at once (when each sits exactly where the other belongs), so selection sort can finish well before its last pass. Second, a bubble-sort pass moves any element at most one place left, so an element that must move $d$ places left forces at least $d$ passes; and insertion sort cannot be finished while a misplaced element still lies in the unexamined part to the right.

**Back to this question.** $[4, 3, 2, 1, 5]$ is $[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]$ with the pairs $1 \leftrightarrow 4$ and $2 \leftrightarrow 3$ exchanged. Selection sort's two swaps undo exactly those two exchanges, so it finishes in two passes. Bubble sort needs three passes because $1$ must travel three places left, one per pass. Insertion sort needs three passes because the $1$ at position 4 is inserted only in pass 3. The answer is **(B)**.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: Bubble sort gives $[3, 2, 1, 4, 5]$ after pass 1 and $[2, 1, 3, 4, 5]$ after pass 2, which is still unsorted. The $1$ moves only one place left per pass and needs a third pass, so (i) does not sort the array in two passes.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: Selection sort swaps $1$ to position 1 in pass 1 ($[1, 3, 2, 4, 5]$) and $2$ to position 2 in pass 2 ($[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]$). The array is sorted after exactly two passes, and (i) and (ii) are not, so "(iii) only" is right.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: (iii) does sort the array in two passes, but (i) does not: bubble sort leaves $[2, 1, 3, 4, 5]$ after two passes. Including (i) makes this choice wrong.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: (iii) does sort the array in two passes, but (ii) does not: insertion sort leaves $[2, 3, 4, 1, 5]$ after two passes, because the $1$ is inserted only in pass 3. Including (ii) makes this choice wrong.

solution.shortcut: Look at where the $1$ is: position 4. Bubble sort moves it left only one place per pass, and insertion sort does not touch it until pass 3, so both need at least three passes. That rules out (i) and (ii), hence (A), (C) and (D). Confirm (iii) with two swaps: $1 \leftrightarrow 4$, then $2 \leftrightarrow 3$.
solution.commonTrap: Picking (A) or (C) because after two bubble-sort passes the two largest values $4$ and $5$ are in place and the array "looks" almost sorted. It is $[2, 1, 3, 4, 5]$, and the $2, 1$ inversion needs a third pass. A second slip is to count insertion sort's starting one-element prefix $[4]$ as a pass. Under any counting, the $1$ at position 4 is not inserted until the third insertion, so insertion sort cannot finish in two passes.

transcription.notes: Single-pass transcription from the official paper rendering; awaiting independent check. The paper lists (i) Bubble sort, (ii) Insertion sort and (iii) Selection sort as an indented list; each item is transcribed as its own paragraph. The bold words ONE and exactly two are kept in bold, and the array is set as math $[4, 3, 2, 1, 5]$.

answerVerification.checkCode:
A0=[4,3,2,1,5]; S=sorted(A0)
def bubble(a):  # left-to-right sweeps
    a=a[:]; out=[]
    for p in range(len(a)-1):
        for j in range(len(a)-1-p):
            if a[j]>a[j+1]: a[j],a[j+1]=a[j+1],a[j]
        out.append(a[:])
    return out
def bubble_rl(a):  # variant: right-to-left sweeps
    a=a[:]; out=[]
    for p in range(len(a)-1):
        for j in range(len(a)-1,p,-1):
            if a[j-1]>a[j]: a[j-1],a[j]=a[j],a[j-1]
        out.append(a[:])
    return out
def insertion(a):
    a=a[:]; out=[]
    for i in range(1,len(a)):
        k=a[i]; j=i-1
        while j>=0 and a[j]>k: a[j+1]=a[j]; j-=1
        a[j+1]=k; out.append(a[:])
    return out
def selection(a):  # standard: minimum of unsorted part to the front
    a=a[:]; out=[]
    for i in range(len(a)-1):
        m=min(range(i,len(a)),key=lambda t:a[t]); a[i],a[m]=a[m],a[i]; out.append(a[:])
    return out
def selection_max(a):  # variant: maximum of unsorted part to the end
    a=a[:]; out=[]
    for i in range(len(a)-1,0,-1):
        m=max(range(i+1),key=lambda t:a[t]); a[i],a[m]=a[m],a[i]; out.append(a[:])
    return out
for name,f in [('bubble',bubble),('bubble_rl',bubble_rl),('insertion',insertion),('selection',selection),('selection_max',selection_max)]:
    ps=f(A0); print(name, ps[:2], 'sorted after exactly two passes:', ps[0]!=S and ps[1]==S)
# bubble [[3,2,1,4,5],[2,1,3,4,5]] False; bubble_rl [[1,4,3,2,5],[1,2,4,3,5]] False
# insertion [[3,4,2,1,5],[2,3,4,1,5]] False; selection [[1,3,2,4,5],[1,2,3,4,5]] True
# selection_max [[4,3,2,1,5],[1,3,2,4,5]] False  -> only (iii) (standard version): option B
answerVerification.notes: A pass-by-pass simulation on [4, 3, 2, 1, 5] shows that only selection sort (standard version, minimum swapped to the front) is sorted after exactly two passes: [1, 3, 2, 4, 5] then [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. Bubble sort (either sweep direction) and insertion sort each need three passes. This gives option B, matching the official key B. The check also shows that the less common max-to-the-end variant of selection sort would need three passes, so the key corresponds to the standard minimum-selecting formulation.
